lead: A parser turns a token string into a parse tree. Top-down parsers start at the start symbol and predict productions. Bottom-up parsers start at the input and reduce handles back to nonterminals. Every compiler front end has one. Only a few universities cover this as an overview.
prereq: You need 4.4 for the grammar-to-PDA construction, and Unit 3 for derivations and parse trees.

blocks.text: Keep a stack holding the unexpanded part of the tree, starting with the start symbol S. Repeat until the stack and the input are both empty.

items: Top of stack is a nonterminal A: choose a production A → α and replace A by the symbols of α, right end deepest.
Top of stack is a terminal a: it must equal the next input symbol. Pop both; a mismatch is an error.
Accept when the stack and the input are both empty.

blocks.text: This is the PDA of 4.4. The production is chosen by one lookahead symbol through a table (predictive parsing), or by the fixed order in which code tries alternatives (recursive descent, one function per nonterminal).

The choice is deterministic only if the grammar allows it. No left recursion: A → A α makes the parser expand A forever. For each nonterminal A, the FIRST sets of its alternatives must be disjoint. FIRST(A) is the set of terminals that can begin a string derived from A. If an alternative can derive ε (a nullable production), FOLLOW(A) must also be disjoint from the FIRST sets of the other alternatives. FOLLOW(A) is the set of terminals that can appear immediately after A. A grammar meeting these conditions is LL(1): scan Left to right, build a Leftmost derivation, with 1 symbol of lookahead.
Keep a stack of grammar symbols, initially empty, and read the input left to right.

items: Shift: push the next input symbol.
Reduce: if the top symbols of the stack spell the body α of a production A → α, pop them and push A.
Accept when the input is finished and the stack holds only S.

blocks.text: The body you reduce is a handle. The reduction list read backwards is a rightmost derivation; the first reduction is the last production of that rightmost derivation.

Table-driven versions are LR: LR(0), SLR(1), LALR(1), canonical LR(1), differing in how much context the table uses. A cell with two entries is a conflict — shift/reduce or reduce/reduce. It means this method cannot handle this grammar; it does not prove the grammar ambiguous.

items: Recursive descent: short hand-written code, good errors, needs an LL grammar.
Table-driven LR: larger class, left recursion included, generator builds the table, bigger tables and cruder errors.
Both are deterministic PDAs; only some context-free languages have a deterministic grammar — see 4.3.

figure.caption: One parse tree for id + id * id, with two orders on each variable: ↓ is when the top-down parser expands it, root first, and ↑ is when the bottom-up parser reduces to it, root last. Both parsers use the same 8 productions.

spec.aria: A parse tree for id + id * id in the grammar E → E + T | T, T → T * F | F, F → id; each variable carries a top-down expansion number 1 to 8 and a bottom-up reduction number 1 to 8.

examples.question: Grammar E → E + T | T, T → T * F | F, F → id. For input id + id * id, give the top-down leftmost derivation with the production used at each step, then the shift-reduce sequence of the bottom-up parser. This grammar is left-recursive, so a real top-down parser would first remove left recursion; the leftmost derivation is shown for comparison with the bottom-up rightmost derivation.
steps: ⇒ id + id * id (F → id). Eight productions, input consumed.
Bottom-up moves: shift id; reduce F→id, T→F, E→T; shift +; shift id; reduce F→id, T→F; shift *; shift id; reduce F→id; reduce T→T*F; reduce E→E+T; accept.
examples.answer: Both parses build the same tree. The 8 reductions read backwards form the rightmost derivation E ⇒ E+T ⇒ E+T*F ⇒ E+T*id ⇒ E+F*id ⇒ E+id*id ⇒ T+id*id ⇒ F+id*id ⇒ id+id*id.

top = "E E+T T+T F+T id+T id+T*F id+F*F id+id*F id+id*id".split()
moves = "shift reduce reduce reduce shift shift reduce reduce shift shift reduce reduce reduce".split()
print(len(top) - 1)
print(moves.count("shift"))
print(moves.count("reduce"))
print(top[-1])

traps: Feeding a left-recursive grammar to a top-down parser: E → E + T calls itself forever. Remove recursion first; bottom-up accepts it.
The top-down stack holds terminals too, not only nonterminals.
Reading reductions forwards as a leftmost derivation. They are a rightmost derivation backwards.
A conflict only says this table method cannot handle the grammar, not that it is ambiguous.

quiz.q: State what a top-down and a bottom-up parser each start from.
quiz.a: Top-down starts at the start symbol; bottom-up starts at the input.

quiz.q: Expand LL(1) and name the four LR variants.
quiz.a: Left to right, leftmost derivation, one lookahead symbol; LR(0), SLR(1), LALR(1), canonical LR(1).

quiz.q: Why does left recursion break a recursive-descent parser?
quiz.a: The function for E calls itself before reading input, so it never returns.

quiz.q: For input id + id * id in the chapter grammar, give the first four shift-reduce moves as (stack, action).
quiz.a: (empty, shift id), (id, reduce F→id), (F, reduce T→F), (T, reduce E→T).

quiz.q: Reading the chapter's reduction list backwards gives which derivation, and why not leftmost?
quiz.a: A rightmost derivation, because each step expands the rightmost remaining nonterminal.

quiz.q: Two grammars generate the same language, one LL(1) and one not. Is the language non-LL(1)?
quiz.a: No. The language is LL(1) because at least one grammar for it is LL(1). A language is non-LL(1) only if no LL(1) grammar generates it.

beyond: Not for the exam. Parser generators such as yacc, bison and ANTLR build these tables from a grammar file. Generalised methods — GLR, Earley, packrat (PEG) — keep several stacks or memoise results. Editors use incremental parsers that reparse only the changed part. Search 'LALR(1) table construction' and 'packrat parsing' to go further.
